title: The Clever Girl Who Saved the Harvest
summary: A young girl remembers her grandma's old trick for protecting date palms and persuades her busy parents to try it before a sudden early cold snap can ruin the family's harvest.
poll: Old family traditions are no longer useful on a modern farm.

versions.title: The Clever Girl Who Saved the Harvest
versions.text:
Noor lived on a farm with palm trees. Her family grew dates. Each year, they picked ripe dates. This was the harvest.

One day, cold air came. It came early. The cold could hurt the young shoots.

Mom and Dad were busy. They did not see the risk.

Noor thought of her grandma. Long ago, Grandma said this: 'Cover the young shoots. Pick the ripe dates now, before the cold comes.'

Noor told her mom and dad. At first, they said no time. Noor did not stop asking. At last, they said yes.

They covered the shoots with cloth. They picked the ripe dates all day.

That night, the cold came. It was very cold!

In the day, the shoots were fine. The dates were safe too. The family was glad. Grandma's old trick saved the harvest.

versions.title: The Clever Girl Who Saved the Harvest
versions.text:
Noor lived with her family on a date palm orchard at the edge of the desert. Every year, when the fruit turned ripe and golden, the family picked it. This busy season, called the harvest, gave the family much of its food and money for the whole year.

One evening, the radio gave a warning. An unusual cold front was moving in earlier than usual. This news worried Noor, because the young, tender shoots on some of the younger trees could be hurt if the cold arrived suddenly.

Her parents were busy with harvest work, checking ladders and fixing baskets. They were so focused on their tasks that they barely heard the warning.

Just then, Noor remembered some advice her grandma had once shared. Years earlier, Grandma used to remind the family, 'When cold arrives early, cover the young shoots to protect them from the chill. Also, pick the ripest dates right away, before the cold weather can reach them.'

Noor explained Grandma's advice to her parents, but at first they said there was no time for extra chores during such a busy week. Noor did not give up. She reminded them that one cold night could ruin months of careful work, and at last her parents agreed to try it.

Working as a team, the family wrapped the young shoots in cloth. Afterward, everyone picked the ripest dates fast, working from early morning until dark.

That night, the cold front finally swept across the orchard. The temperature dropped sharply.

The next morning, the covered shoots were still healthy. The dates the family had picked the day before were safe too. Everyone felt proud that Grandma's old advice had protected their harvest.

One evening, the radio announced that an unusually early cold front was moving in. It was coming sooner than farmers in the area usually expected. The news worried Noor right away. The young, tender shoots on several of the orchard's younger trees could be badly hurt if a sudden freeze struck before anyone was ready.

Her parents, though, were busy with harvest work. They checked ladders, fixed baskets, and looked at each tree row by row. They were working so hard that they barely noticed the warning from the radio in the kitchen.

Just then, Noor remembered some advice her grandma had shared years earlier. Grandma used to remind everyone, 'When cold weather arrives early, cover the young shoots with cloth to protect them from the chill. Also, pick the ripest dates right away, before the cold air can reach them.'

Noor carefully explained Grandma's old advice to her parents. At first they said there simply was not time for extra chores during such a busy week. Noor refused to give up. She gently reminded them that one freezing night could undo months of careful work. At last her parents agreed to give the idea a real try.

Working together as a team, the family wrapped the young shoots in cloth to shield them from the cold. Afterward, everyone picked the ripest dates as fast as they could. They worked from early morning until the sky grew dark.

That night, the cold front finally swept across the orchard. The temperature dropped sharply and stayed low for hours.

The next morning, the covered shoots were still healthy. The dates the family had gathered the day before were completely safe. Everyone felt proud and thankful that Grandma's old advice had protected their harvest.

versions.title: The Clever Girl Who Saved the Harvest
versions.text:
Noor's family tended a date palm orchard near a small village in Saudi Arabia's Qassim region, where long rows of towering palms stretched toward the horizon. Each year, once the fruit ripened to a deep golden color, the family gathered for the harvest, a season that shaped much of the household's income and food supply, since the yield could vary depending on the weather.

One evening, the weather forecast on the radio announced that an unusually early cold front was sweeping down from the north, arriving weeks sooner than local farmers typically expected. The news alarmed Noor at once, because young shoots have not yet developed the thicker bark that shields older branches from frost.

Her parents, however, were absorbed in ordinary harvest preparations, checking ladders and mending baskets, and barely registered the forecast from the kitchen radio.

Just then, Noor recalled some practical advice her grandma had shared years earlier. Grandma used to remind the family that whenever cold weather arrived early, they should cover the young shoots with cloth to preserve their warmth, and harvest the ripest dates right away, before the cold air could reach them.

Noor explained her grandma's advice to her parents, but at first they protested that there was simply no time for extra chores during such a demanding week. Rather than give up, Noor worked to persuade them, pointing out that a single freezing night could undo months of patient labor. Eventually, her parents agreed to give the old method a try.

Working together as a team, the family wrapped the young shoots in cloth, tying each covering so the wind could not tear it loose. Afterward, everyone raced to pick the ripest dates before dark.

That night, the cold front swept across the orchard, and temperatures dropped and stayed low for hours.

The next morning, the covered shoots were healthy, and the dates gathered the day before stayed safe. The family's entire yield had been preserved. From that day forward, Noor's parents listened more closely whenever she mentioned something from her grandma, recognizing that old traditions could still matter, even on a modern farm.

wrong.D: Noor was trying to help her parents, not showing dislike for them.

questions.stem: What happened because the family covered the shoots and picked the dates early?

The shoots and dates were saved
The trees grew much taller
The family lost the harvest in the cold
questions.why: Because the family covered the shoots and picked the ripe dates early, both were safe when the cold arrived that night.

wrong.C: The story does not say the trees grew taller.
wrong.D: The family did not lose the harvest; they saved it.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us what Grandma used to say?
options: To show Grandma liked to talk
To explain how to grow trees
To show where Noor's idea came from
To describe Grandma's old house in the village
questions.why: The author includes Grandma's old advice to show the reader exactly where Noor's idea for saving the harvest came from.

wrong.A: The story is not about Grandma liking to talk.
wrong.B: The story does not explain how to grow new trees.
wrong.D: The story does not describe Grandma's house.

LOW.prompt: Would you cover the shoots and pick the dates early if you were Noor's parent? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think the parents were right to try Grandma's trick. The radio said cold air was coming early, and young shoots can be hurt by sudden cold. Noor remembered that Grandma said to cover the shoots and pick the ripe dates early. Because the family did this, the shoots and the dates were safe the next morning.

keyWords.definition: a piece of land where fruit trees are grown
keyWords.example: We picked apples in my uncle's orchard.

keyWords.definition: to keep someone or something safe from harm

Please remind me to call my friend after school.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Noor's family decided to sell their land to a neighbor and move to the city
Noor's parents refuse to ever listen to her, so the harvest is lost to the cold
Noor remembers Grandma's advice and persuades her parents to protect the harvest
The story mainly describes different baskets and how the farmers use them each day
questions.why: The story is about Noor remembering her grandma's advice and convincing her parents to use it to protect the harvest from an early cold front.

wrong.A: The family does not sell any land in the story.
wrong.B: The parents eventually agree to try Noor's idea.
wrong.D: The story is not about describing baskets.

questions.stem: Why was the cold front especially dangerous for the young shoots?
options: They are usually eaten by birds
They grow quite far away from the orchard
They are the orchard's tallest trees
They have thinner bark than older limbs
questions.why: Young shoots do not yet have the thicker bark that protects older branches from the cold.

wrong.B: The shoots grow inside the orchard, not far away.
wrong.C: Young shoots are small, not the tallest trees.

questions.stem: What two things did Grandma advise doing when cold arrives early?
options: Cover the shoots and harvest ripe dates right away
Water the trees more and pick weeds each day, early in the morning
Call the neighbors and buy more cloth, too
Move the young trees indoors and wait a week

wrong.B: The story does not mention watering more or picking weeds.
wrong.C: The story does not mention calling neighbors.
wrong.D: Palm trees cannot be moved indoors.

questions.stem: In the story, the word orchard means —
options: a kind of basket for picking fruit
a simple tool for covering plants
a place where fruit trees grow
a type of sudden cold wind

wrong.B: An orchard is not a tool.
wrong.D: An orchard is not a kind of wind.

questions.stem: Why were Noor's parents at first unwilling to try Grandma's advice?
options: They did not trust old traditions from the village
They simply did not like cloth on their trees
They wanted to sell their orchard before the winter
They thought there was no time for extra chores
questions.why: The parents were busy with harvest preparations and said there was simply no time for extra chores during such a demanding week.

wrong.A: The story does not say they disbelieved old traditions.
wrong.B: The story does not say they disliked cloth.
wrong.C: The family was not trying to sell the orchard.

questions.stem: What can you infer about Grandma from the story?
options: She never once visited the orchard when she was young
She had learned useful ways to protect crops from cold
She did not like dates, so she did not grow them
She was afraid of cold weather and stayed inside
questions.why: Grandma's advice about covering shoots and harvesting early suggests she had learned practical, useful methods from years of experience.

wrong.A: The advice suggests she knew the orchard well.
wrong.C: There is no reason to think she disliked dates.
wrong.D: Her advice shows she knew how to deal with cold, not that she feared it.

questions.stem: Why was the family's harvest safe after the cold front arrived?
options: The cold front turned out to be weak, so it did not matter
They had already sold all their dates at the market
They had covered the shoots and picked dates early
The radio was simply wrong about the cold, and no frost came
questions.why: Because the family covered the young shoots and picked the ripest dates early, both the shoots and the dates stayed safe through the cold night.

wrong.A: The story says the temperature dropped sharply, so the cold front was real.
wrong.B: The family had not sold their dates; they picked and kept them.
wrong.D: The radio's warning about the cold front turned out to be correct.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the events in the story?
options: By comparing two different orchards, one old and one new, in the same town
By listing random facts about date palms and the places they grow
By describing the orchard from the present back to the past, step by step
In time order: the warning, Noor's memory, the work, and the result
questions.why: The story follows the events in time order, from the radio warning, to Noor remembering the advice, to the family's work, to the safe outcome the next morning.

wrong.A: The story does not compare two orchards.
wrong.B: The story is a narrative, not a list of facts.
wrong.C: The story moves forward in time, not backward.

MID.prompt: Explain how Noor convinced her parents to try her grandma's advice, and why it worked. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Noor convinced her parents.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Noor convinced her parents by not giving up, even though they were busy and said no time at first. She reminded them that a single freezing night could ruin months of work on the orchard, which helped them see why trying Grandma's advice mattered. Because they finally agreed to cover the young shoots and pick the ripest dates early, the whole harvest stayed safe when the cold front arrived that night. It worked because Grandma's old method was based on real experience with sudden cold weather.

keyWords.definition: a statement about what the weather, or some other event, is expected to be like in the future
keyWords.example: The forecast predicted heavy rain for the weekend.

keyWords.definition: to keep something safe or in good condition so it is not lost or damaged

keyWords.definition: a belief, custom, or way of doing something that is passed down over many years

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: An early cold front threatens the harvest, but a girl's memory of old advice persuades her parents to protect it
Dates are simply impossible to grow in Saudi Arabia, since the weather is too cold, and the farm will fail
Noor's parents never trust her again after she wakes them up at night, so the harvest is lost to the frost
The story is mainly about the history of date farming in the oasis, and the cold front matters little
questions.why: The story centers on Noor recalling her grandma's traditional advice and persuading her parents to use it to protect the orchard's yield from an unexpected cold front.

wrong.B: The story shows a family successfully growing dates.
wrong.C: By the end, the parents listen to Noor more closely, not less.
wrong.D: The story is a narrative about one harvest, not a history of farming.

questions.stem: Why were the young shoots especially at risk from the sudden freeze?
options: They had been planted too close together in the rows
They lacked the thicker bark that shields older branches
They had already been harvested that day by the workers

wrong.C: Shoots are not harvested; dates are.
wrong.D: The story does not mention shade.

questions.stem: According to the forecast, how did this cold front compare with what farmers usually expected?
options: It was described as far milder than usual
It arrived weeks earlier than usual
It was expected months in advance
It actually never arrived
questions.why: The forecast announced that the cold front was arriving weeks sooner than local farmers typically expected.

wrong.A: The cold front caused temperatures to plunge sharply, so it was not mild.
wrong.C: The forecast came suddenly, not months in advance.
wrong.D: The cold front did arrive, as described that night.

questions.stem: In the story, to persuade someone means to —

to convince them with good reasons
to argue with them very angrily
to copy their actions exactly as shown
questions.why: Noor worked to persuade her parents by calmly giving them good reasons to try the old method, meaning she convinced them to agree.

wrong.A: Persuading someone involves engaging with them, not ignoring them.
wrong.C: Noor reasoned gently rather than arguing angrily.
wrong.D: Persuading is about convincing, not copying actions.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why Noor's parents eventually agreed to try the old method?
options: They had planned to follow Grandma's way
Noor's calm, steady reasoning wore down their doubts
A neighbor convinced them to try it instead
The radio forecast suddenly changed its prediction
questions.why: In the story, Noor's calm, patient reasoning is what changed her parents' minds.

wrong.C: No neighbor appears in the story.
wrong.D: The forecast's prediction did not change; the cold front arrived as predicted.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order.
options: The forecast is heard, parents agree, shoots are covered, cold front arrives
The cold front arrives, the forecast is heard, shoots are covered, parents agree
Parents agree, forecast heard, cold front arrives, shoots covered
Shoots are covered, cold front arrives, parents agree, forecast heard
questions.why: The family first hears the forecast, then the parents agree to try the method after Noor persuades them, then they cover the shoots, and finally the cold front arrives that night.

wrong.C: The parents agree only after hearing the forecast and being persuaded.
wrong.D: The shoots are covered before the cold front arrives, not after.

questions.stem: What does the family's experience suggest about traditional farming knowledge?

It should fully replace weather forecasts

It only really matters for flowers

wrong.B: The forecast was still useful for warning the family; it was not replaced.
wrong.D: The tradition in the story is about saving a date harvest, not flowers.

questions.stem: Why does the author include Noor's insistence that the credit belonged to her grandma?
options: To suggest Noor felt no pride
To show Grandma still worked on the farm
To argue children should not help with farming
To show how valuable old knowledge can be
questions.why: By having Noor credit her late grandma, the author highlights how traditional knowledge passed down through generations can still matter deeply.

wrong.A: Noor did feel quietly proud, even while crediting her grandma.
wrong.B: Grandma's advice came from years earlier; the story does not show her working on the farm.
wrong.C: The story shows Noor's help was valuable, not discouraged.

HIGH.prompt: Do you agree that old family traditions can still be useful on a modern farm? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Noor's grandma's advice.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that old family traditions can still be useful on a modern farm. In the story, Grandma's advice to cover young shoots and harvest early came from years of practical experience, and it turned out to be exactly what the orchard needed when an unusual cold front arrived. Someone might argue that modern forecasts and equipment make old traditions unnecessary, but the forecast alone did not protect the trees — it was Noor's memory of her grandma's method that actually preserved the yield. This shows that scientific tools and traditional knowledge can work well together, rather than one replacing the other.
